rows.searchedFor: can I do some paid freelance work outside my job here?
rows.answer:
A few hours a month on a paid side gig is acceptable, and side gigs should by default be something you work on in your personal time and should not impact your PostHog work.[1]

- The handbook says PostHog is ok with you earning money on the side, but not with it being your main focus and PostHog being just a paycheck.[2]
- What makes something an appropriate side gig is its impact on your work and the amount of time involved.[3]
- The handbook says it doesn't think you can look after yourself properly while going above and beyond for PostHog beyond a certain level of time/energy commitment to a side gig, but it is happy for you to spend a little time on them each week.[4]
- If you want a side gig to become your full time work one day, let PostHog know so they can create a plan.[5]
- PostHog currently doesn't offer part time work as an option.[2]

rows.searchedFor: a big prospect wants a feature promised by Q3 written into their contract - is that ok?
rows.answer:
No, the handbook says PostHog doesn't do this: we don't contract deliverables, and we especially don't contract to provide deliverables by a certain date, because on principle a single customer shouldn't be forcing us to build something.[1]

Related points from the handbook:
- If PostHog has to compromise on these principles to close a deal, it will walk away, which it can do because of a strong growth engine with ICP customers.[2]
- PostHog will build things for a big customer as long as it is confident they won't be the only user of that thing.[3]
- Customers need to try PostHog before they expect changes, and the handbook says feedback is welcome but big requirement documents from people who haven't used the product are not.[4]

rows.searchedFor: how does a YC founder get a desk at Hogpatch?
rows.answer:
A YC founder can't apply for Hogpatch: it is invite-only and isn't open to the whole batch, and PostHog handpicks a few YC companies to join when space opens up.[1] There is a waitlist, but you can't apply, because founders are handpicked when there's room.[2]

Once invited:
- Judy, the office manager, sends you and your cofounders a digital wallet pass, which gives 24/7 self-service access.[3]
- Desks and phone booths have no booking system, so you just grab a spot when you arrive.[4]
- Each invite lasts 3 months.[5]

rows.searchedFor: why did US customers lose their older Logs data in February?
rows.answer:
A routine mutation run on Feb 19 to materialize an index triggered a bug in ClickHouse's zero-copy replication, which caused one of the replicas to erroneously believe all of the data parts in the database were no longer referenced.[1]

- From 11:02 to 19:40 UTC, the replicas deleted all of the data stored in S3 for the entire database. Data is only moved to S3 after 24 hours, and most queries are for recent data, so the volume of query errors was low and no automated alarms triggered.[2]
- PostHog lacked monitoring for the integrity of "cold" data in S3. Its alerts focused on ingestion lag, query latency, and error rates on active queries, and the deletion happened silently in the background, so dashboards stayed "green" until a node restart forced a consistency check.[3]
- At 19:40 a node crashed and restarted, but it failed to start because of the large volume of missing data, and engineers then discovered that the vast majority of S3-backed data was missing.[4]
- At 21:45 the data was determined most likely unrecoverable, and disaster recovery procedures started.[5]

The result was the loss of data collected more than 3 days ago in the US region, affecting only the Logs product.[6] Kafka's 3 days of retention prevented total data loss for recent activity.[7]

rows.searchedFor: Did PostHog recover any of the older Logs data that US customers lost in February?
rows.answer:
The handbook says the February 19th incident caused the loss of Logs data collected more than 3 days ago in the US region[1]. Engineers determined that the data was most likely unrecoverable, so disaster recovery procedures started[2].

What was restored was the most recent data. The decision was made to cut over to a new table and restore data from Kafka, which has 3 days of retention[3]. The backfill from Kafka history began on Feb 20 at 10:05 and completed at 12:21[4]. The handbook notes that the 3-day Kafka retention saved them from total data loss for recent activity[5].

rows.searchedFor: we're launching a beta soon - when do we need to start tracking which users are interested in our product?
rows.answer:
The handbook says you should start tracking product intents as soon as your product is in any sort of public beta, so that data is collected for later when a good activation metric is being determined[1]. It adds that collecting product intents should be a precursor to any sort of public release[2], so set it up before your beta goes public.

Separately, if you mean tracking interest via sign-ups, the handbook says adding items to the coming soon menu early lets you gauge interest in a new feature via sign-ups and ensures betas can have sample users ready from the moment they launch[3]. Users who registered interest during the Concept stage can then opt in once the item moves to beta.[4]

rows.searchedFor: which of my accounts are big enough to be worth visiting in person?
rows.answer:
The handbook gives two thresholds, so which of your accounts qualify depends on which you apply.

- In-person visits work best for accounts paying or likely to pay $50k+/year where you've identified specific opportunities for expansion, are navigating renewal conversations, or need to overcome significant technical or organizational hurdles.[1]
- Generally you should be trying to regularly see customers in your book of business who are $100k+ annually, or could get there.[2]
- You should match the cadence of in-person meetings to contract size: more regular for Very Large, less regular for Large.[3]

The handbook calls visits a high-effort, high-reward play to use strategically.[1] It also says your intuition and experience should ultimately guide who you meet.[4]

The handbook can't tell me which specific accounts are in your book. You'd need to check their current or likely annual spend against these thresholds.

rows.searchedFor: how do I pull the posthog org IDs for all my accounts out of salesforce?
rows.answer:
Query PostHog's data warehouse to pull Salesforce data and create a CSV of all PostHog organization IDs for accounts you own.[1]

The handbook gives this SQL query:

- SELECT DISTINCT posthog_org_id_c, NULL as empty_column FROM salesforce.account WHERE owner_id = 'your_salesforce_id'[2]
- You can find your Salesforce ID by going to your profile and copying the text in the website URL after "/User/".[2]
- Export the results via CSV.[2]

The empty column is there so there are commas as delimiters for the org IDs, which lets you copy and paste all the org IDs directly into a filter input text field.[2]

rows.searchedFor: how can I see what posthog is doing on a customer's live site?
rows.answer:
The handbook describes two ways to check how PostHog is being called on a customer's site (specifically, whether a reverse proxy is set up):

- If the customer uses session replay, go to the appropriate replay video, select Activity > Inspector > Doctor, search for "config", look for PostHog Config, and expand api_host to see whether the URL is one of PostHog's domains (us.i.posthog.com or eu.i.posthog.com) or one of the customer's own.[1]
- If the customer isn't using session replay, add ?__posthog_debug=true to a URL where PostHog is being called, pull up the console logs, type posthog.config, and look for the api_host property.[2]

If neither method is available because the customer isn't using session replay and the hosted site isn't publicly accessible, you can ask the customer on the discovery call.[3]

rows.searchedFor: How can I check if a customer has set up a reverse proxy for PostHog on their live site?
rows.answer:
Check the customer's api_host setting to see whether it points to PostHog's domains or their own.[1] There are two ways, depending on whether they use session replay:

- With session replay, open the relevant replay video, select Activity > Inspector > Doctor, and search for "config". Find PostHog Config, expand api_host, and see whether the URL is one of PostHog's domains (us.i.posthog.com or eu.i.posthog.com) or one of the customer's own.[2]
- Without session replay, add ?__posthog_debug=true to a URL where PostHog is being called, open the console logs, type posthog.config, and look at the api_host property.[3]

If api_host shows us.i.posthog or eu.i.posthog, they are not using a reverse proxy.[4]

If neither method works because the customer isn't using session replay and the hosted site isn't publicly accessible, you can ask the customer on the discovery call.[5]

Two more checks: events sent through a managed or non-managed reverse proxy should populate the "Library custom API host" property, and host mapping and domains can potentially be seen in Metabase. You should verify the setup with the customer.[6]
